in-depth.title: How Example Widgets Inc. Plans Its Widget Supply
in-depth.dek: A synthetic walkthrough of forecasting, buffers and the trade-offs behind them.

blocks.md: Example Widgets Inc. sells **widgets** through three channels. Its supply plan decides how many to build each quarter, and a bad plan either strands cash in inventory or leaves shelves empty.
The plan balances two costs: holding too much stock and running out.

eli5.title: Widgets, explained simply
eli5.dek: Why a company keeps a few extra widgets on the shelf.

blocks.md: It is like buying snacks for a party when you do not know exactly how many friends will come.
Example Widgets Inc. has to guess how many widgets people will buy before they buy them.
A small pile of extra widgets means nobody leaves empty-handed, but extras cost money to store.
More online shoppers means a bigger pile is needed.

section-expand.heading: How the forecast is built, step by step

blocks.md: The forecast starts from last quarter's orders and smooths them with a moving average so one unusual week does not swing the plan.

section-reexplain.heading: How the forecast is built, another way

blocks.md: Think of the forecast as an average of recent weeks: it follows the trend without chasing every bump.
Forecasting is like a weather report for orders: usually close, never exact. The analogy stops working because customers, unlike clouds, respond to prices.

section-deeper.heading: How the forecast is built, in depth

blocks.md: A moving average lags turning points. When online demand accelerates, the forecast underestimates it for a few weeks, which is exactly when the safety stock is consumed.
Guessing orders is like guessing how many pancakes the family will eat on Sunday.

summary.title: How Example Widgets Inc. Plans Its Widget Supply
summary.summary: A synthetic explainer on how a widget maker forecasts demand by channel and sizes its safety stock.

blocks.md: Example Widgets Inc. sells **widgets** through three channels, and online is now the fastest-growing one. Its supply plan decides how many to build each quarter, and a bad plan either strands cash in inventory or leaves shelves empty.
About 6% of online orders come back, so the plan now tracks the **sell-through rate**: widgets kept by buyers, not just widgets shipped.
Example Widgets Inc. has to guess how many widgets people will buy before they buy them, and more people now shop online.
Sometimes people send a widget back. The company counts those too, so it does not make too many.

glossary.explanation: The share of shipped widgets that buyers keep.
